title: QPrompt-R1: Real-Time Reasoning for Domain-Generalized Semantic Segmentation via Group-Relative Query Alignment
one_liner: A real-time semantic segmentation model uses learnable question-phrases pinned at the final layer, then aligns them to image features using group-relative supervision to keep working across camera shifts.
lead: When a car's camera moves from a sunny street to a rainy tunnel, the learned rules for recognizing road signs often fall apart. Semantic segmentation (the task of labeling every pixel) faces two competing demands: speed (processing at 54 frames per second for self-driving) and stubbornness (working when the camera or lighting shifts). This paper unites both by injecting learnable queries only at the final layer and teaching them to align with image regions using group-relative rewards, so the model sees new conditions and adapts without slowing down.

problem.h2: Speed and reliability are locked in conflict
paras: Semantic segmentation in robotics and self-driving cars must identify every pixel (road, sidewalk, sign, person) in real-time. A naive approach: use a large model to encode the image deeply and then decode predictions—this is accurate but slow. A faster approach: use a lean model that runs quickly but breaks when the camera hardware changes or lighting flips from day to night, because lean models memorize exact patterns in the training camera's output (its color tone, blur profile, sensor noise) rather than learning the underlying visual concepts.

Most papers solve one or the other. Methods that work across camera shifts (called domain generalization) add extra computation to extract stable features, killing real-time speed. Fast methods strip down the model to run in 17 milliseconds, but this brittleness means a model trained on sunny footage fails on rainy footage, even though humans see roads and cars in both.

callout.html: No existing model achieves both 54 frames per second AND stable predictions when the camera shifts.

steps.text: A pre-trained image-reading model (vision transformer) processes the photograph into feature arrays.

steps.b: Queries injected only at final block
steps.text: Instead of decoding layer-by-layer, a small set of learnable 'question' embeddings (queries) join only the last transformer block.

steps.b: Single alignment step between queries and features
steps.text: Queries and image features are aligned once: each query finds the image regions it matches, with no separate decoder network.

steps.b: Group-relative rewards guide alignment during training
steps.text: Training uses a group-relative objective: for each group of similar images, a query is rewarded for matching features more similarly within the group than across domain boundaries.

steps.b: Inference: 54 FPS, stable predictions across cameras
steps.text: At test time, the learned queries run in parallel with no per-image optimization, achieving speed and generalization simultaneously.

paras: The paper changes where learnable queries (small trainable lists of numbers that 'ask' the image for specific features) are injected. Instead of distributing them across multiple decoder layers, queries are inserted only at the final transformer block (a neural network layer that reads images as pixel patches). This radical deletion of intermediate layers eliminates the computational overhead that makes domain-stable models slow.
object.object: Decoder depth: from 5+ layers to a single alignment.

hidden.name: Group-relative alignment score
paras: The paper introduces group-relative alignment: a hidden quantity measuring how consistently a learnable query matches image features within a group of similar images (e.g., from one camera model or lighting condition), compared to matches across groups. Traditional methods measure absolute correctness (Is the pixel label right?); this measures relative consistency (Do the same features activate the query similarly across the domain group?).

During training, the model estimates this score by sampling image triplets: an anchor image, a neighbor from the same domain group, and an outlier from a different domain. If a query fires strongly on similar features in the anchor and neighbor but weakly on the outlier, its alignment score rises. This group-relative supervision teaches queries to ignore which camera or light is present and focus only on the semantic content.

heat.caption: Darker means stronger alignment within group. Borders highlight stable features that queries learn to recognize across domain shifts.

reads.html: A query learns not to memorize 'what the road looks like under this exact camera,' but instead learns 'the pattern that always shows up when the road is visible, even if the camera or light changes.'

Group-relative query alignment is a supervision objective that increases when query responses are more similar for images within a domain group than for images across domain boundaries, measured via contrastive ranking losses on triplets.

mechanism.h2: Why encoding-only plus group-relative reward works
paras: The core mechanism has two parts. First, removing the decoder layers cuts computational cost drastically: instead of 5-10 transformer blocks (neural network layers that read images as patches) processing features through progressively smaller representations, queries align directly with features from the encoder's final block. This slim design runs at 54 frames per second.

Second, group-relative supervision teaches queries to be stable across domain shifts without explicit multi-domain training data. Here is the chain: when the model trains on triplets (an image from camera A, another from A, and one from camera B), it rewards queries that respond similarly to the two A images but differently to the B image. Over many such triplets, queries internalize a rule: 'respond to the semantic content, not the camera artifacts.' This is why the model generalizes to new cameras at test time—it has learned invariance from relative consistency, not from seeing every possible camera.

The alignment step itself is efficient: each query is a small learned list of numbers that dot-products (a simple arithmetic operation) with image features once, producing a heatmap of where that query's semantic concept lives. No recurrent decoding, no iterative refinement. The speed follows directly from this architectural simplicity; the stability follows from training with group-relative rewards, which naturally extract domain-invariant patterns.

stages.s: Vision transformer encoder: extract feature arrays
Inject learnable queries at final block only
Single query-feature alignment: dot product to heatmaps
Group-relative reward during training: compare within vs. across domains
Semantic segmentation mask, 54 FPS, stable across camera shifts

math.words: For each query, the training loss compares how aligned the query is within a domain group versus across domain boundaries. The reward is based on a ranking: how many images from a different domain have lower query activation than the neighbor from the same domain.
math.equation: L_GRQA = 1/N * sum_i max(0, 1 + sim(q, out_shift_i) - sim(q, out_same_i))
symbols: dot product (how much query and feature match), ranges 0 to 1
image features from the same domain group as anchor
image features from a different domain (e.g., different camera)
no penalty if the same-group match wins; penalty if different-domain match is stronger
group-relative alignment loss (minimize this during training)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Query fires on a road-sign feature list of numbers.
Anchor image (sunny camera A): query matches road sign, sim = 0.8.
Neighbor image (also sunny, camera A): query matches road sign similarly, sim = 0.79.
Outlier image (rainy, camera B): same road sign but rainy, query matches less, sim = 0.6.
Loss for this triplet: max(0, 1 + 0.6 - 0.79) = max(0, 0.81) = 0.81.
Training nudges query to respond more strongly on camera-invariant road-sign patterns.
If outlier had won (sim = 0.9), penalty would be max(0, 1 + 0.9 - 0.79) = 1.11, much bigger.

math.note: The formula penalizes queries that are fooled by domain shift; it rewards invariance by training queries to see through camera and lighting changes and recognize the same road or sign reliably.

charts.title: Slow stable baseline (existing methods)
charts.note: Adds decoder layers for stability but sacrifices real-time speed. Generalization is partial.

charts.title: QPrompt-R1 (this paper)
charts.note: Achieves strong performance on new cameras (synthetic-to-real, real-to-real) while meeting real-time frame rate demands.

items.b: Queries memorize camera artifacts if group boundaries are not clear.
items.html: Group-relative alignment only works if the training data clearly marks which images belong to the same domain group. If domain labels are missing or noisy, queries can still memorize camera-specific patterns instead of learning semantic invariance.

The method requires explicit triplet sampling from the training set. If the dataset has only a few cameras or lighting conditions, the triplets may not cover enough domain variation, and the learned invariance will be narrow.

items.b: Extreme domain shift still breaks alignment.
items.html: If the test camera is radically different from all training cameras (e.g. a thermal camera when training only on RGB), even group-relative rewards cannot help queries generalize, because the underlying data (thermal radiation versus light reflectance) is fundamentally different; no amount of alignment training can bridge an input type that was never seen.
With clear domain labels and diverse training cameras, group-relative alignment teaches queries stable, semantic invariants that transfer to unseen cameras without retraining.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: A simple runnable demo would train QPrompt-R1 on a subset of Cityscapes (urban scenes from one camera model), then evaluate performance on SYNTHIA (synthetic urban scenes that simulate a different camera's rendering). Measure: how well does the model segment roads, sidewalks, and cars in SYNTHIA despite training only on Cityscapes? A good baseline for comparison is a standard vision transformer-based segmentation model (a neural network that reads images as patches) trained on the same Cityscapes subset. The demo should show that QPrompt-R1 maintains high accuracy on SYNTHIA while baseline accuracy drops, proving that group-relative alignment teaches true generalization. Also measure inference time: QPrompt-R1 should process the SYNTHIA images at 50+ FPS, while the baseline or other methods that work across cameras run at 10-20 FPS.
demo.closing: The demo must show that removing decoder layers and training with group-relative rewards delivers both faster inference and better cross-camera accuracy, not a trade-off between the two, because the group-relative approach extracts invariant semantic patterns while the slim architecture eliminates computational bottlenecks that slow down reliable methods.
